A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LiveBench. Their complete main texts and appendices, including tables, figures, equations, and examples, support reliable comparison. Changed benchmark settings require care when comparing scores.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 49 models, benchmark correlations, LLM-judging experiments, and Olympiad difficulty analyses.

after.justification: v2 reports an updated 40-model leaderboard, new task/category correlation and monthly-update analyses, and retained judging and difficulty experiments.

M1.justification: Beyond v1's monthly-refresh framework, v2 introduces a rolling private question subset with one-month delayed release (Section 2.7) and reports scoring-function refinements followed by rescoring models (Appendix A.5). These refine contamination control and grading while retaining the central task-generation and objective-scoring framework.

E1.justification: v2 adds 50 handwritten spatial-reasoning questions about intersections and orientations of 2D/3D shapes and extends code completion to easy LeetCode problems. These are limited extensions within the retained six domains. Replacing 2023 Olympiad questions with 2024 questions preserves the existing proof-completion task.

E2.justification: The main comparison roster changes substantially from 49 models in v1 Table 3 to 40 in v2 Table 2. Actual additions include o1-preview, o1-mini, Llama-3.1-405B, Gemma-2-27B, and Qwen2.5-Coder-32B; older DeepSeek-v2, Qwen1.5, and Starling entries leave this leaderboard. Some older models remain in retained appendix experiments.

E3.justification: v2 introduces longitudinal evaluation across benchmark updates and revises question composition: coding-generation/completion counts change from 50/38 to 78/50, and easy completion problems omit 30–70% of solutions. It also permits model-specific temperature exceptions. The documented judge prompt changes from a 1–10 rating to binary correctness, although unchanged result tables do not establish a rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses examine category/task correlations, models' relative strengths through regression residuals, and ranking stability and difficulty across monthly updates (Sections 3.2 and 3.4; Appendix A.1). The earlier judge-error and Olympiad masking-difficulty analyses remain; their relocation does not constitute new evidence.

E5.justification: v2 adds reported standard errors alongside category/task correlations in Tables 5–6 and regression statistics in Figure 3. Both versions already report 95% bootstrap confidence intervals for leaderboard scores. No additional repeated-run or seed counts are specified.

E6.justification: Leaderboard results are substantially replaced: v1 Table 1 is led by June Claude-3.5-Sonnet at 61.2, whereas v2 Table 1 is led by o1-preview at 64.7. The retained June Claude model scores 58.2 on the revised benchmark, not a demonstrated same-setting decline. New findings include update rank correlations above 0.997; the earlier judging and Olympiad-difficulty numbers remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The column-type annotation definitions and Equations (1)–(2), Boolean formulation of Web of Lies, and mathematical scoring descriptions are retained. The new contamination discussion is conceptual rather than a new formal definition, theorem, proof, or derivation.

C1.justification: The central contamination claim is materially narrowed: v1's title and framing promise 'contamination-free' evaluation and immunity, while v2 uses 'contamination-limited' and resistance, explicitly acknowledging likely contamination in Appendix A.7. Monthly updates also change from a future commitment to a claimed implemented capability. The three-part benchmark contribution otherwise remains.

C2.justification: v2 distinguishes test leakage from task-distribution similarity and acknowledges contamination from older coding and lightly modified AMC questions. It adds substantive discussion of formatting and instruction-following confounds in automatic grading. The judge experiment is reframed as preliminary and sensitive to alternative prompting, and new interpretations address category relationships and update stability.

D1.justification: Sections 6 and Appendices A.4–A.6 substantially expand documentation of accepted answer formats, model setup, manual checking, rescoring, version control, and question maintenance. v2 specifies delayed question release and undisclosed question-generation code, qualifying v1's broad release statements. Token statistics and estimated evaluation costs are also updated.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion of Omni-MATH, newer contamination studies, schema-matching applications, and newer model references. Its static-leaderboard examples shift toward Big-Bench Hard and MMLU-Pro. These update the surrounding literature while retaining the main positioning against static benchmarks, LLM/human judging, and coding-only LiveCodeBench.

P1.justification: The main narrative sequence and much of the task-description prose remain. v2 edits selected explanations and results discussion, moves the detailed judge-ablation discussion into the appendix, and adds clearly labelled maintenance, reproducibility, ethics, and appendix subsections. Title, authorship information, and citation style also change.

P2.justification: v2 substantially revises the visual presentation through an ICLR layout, new correlation heatmaps and residual plots, and new correlation, model-reference, task-summary, and update-automation tables. Figure 1 is revised and supplemented by a full leaderboard plot in the appendix. Existing judging and difficulty tables are redistributed closer to their discussions.

improvement.justification: v2 improves scientific candor about contamination, documents grading and maintenance controls, and adds evidence about task relationships and update stability. These gains are limited by unreleased question-generation code and unreconciled reporting: Section 3.1 misidentifies Table 1's runner-up, and Section 3.2 calls math_comp the strongest correlate although Table 6 ranks Web of Lies higher. The net improvement is useful but qualified.
